messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Two years ago, at forty-three, Elena collapsed during a Saturday dinner service. By the time paramedics reached her, septic shock had pushed her blood pressure into the red. She remembers the violent shivering, the taste of copper, and the frantic hands of the emergency team as her lungs stopped responding to her commands. When she woke in the ICU, tubes anchored her arms and chest, and a ventilator breathed for her. The experience felt so extreme and complete across all her senses that it was hard for her to believe it actually happened to her, yet the grief on recall still flooded her kitchen whenever she saw a respiratory therapist. In the weeks that followed, her body would react to danger before her mind could catch up, her heart hammering the moment she leaned over a simmering stockpot. This physiological alarm kept her unable to relax, even when she finally returned home to her partner. Her body reacted as if she were still trapped in that ICU bed, which cemented her conviction that her body was an enemy. She was certain her physical vulnerability was permanent, that the illness had fractured her nervous system beyond repair. Because her body kept signaling fatal threat, she stopped trusting her own physiology, and this mistrust inevitably pulled the hospital memories back to the surface. Every time a flashback pulled her back to the ventilator’s hiss, her body would lock up again before she could think, and that raw physiological alarm would inevitably trigger another wave of overwhelming grief, confirming her conviction that she was permanently damaged and emotionally hollowed out. Because her negative appraisals convinced her she would never feel normal emotions again, she deliberately numbed her feelings and avoided positive events. That same conviction that her body was permanently vulnerable kept her nervous system locked in a state of hyperarousal, which in turn kept the hospital memories vivid. Her belief that she was physically compromised sharpened her focus on illness-related cues, sustaining the intrusions. The overwhelming grief that followed each sensory reliving of the event drove her to delay sleep until 3 a.m. and isolate from joy. Her inability to relax at work forced her to adopt emotional numbing as a way to function, and by refusing to unwind or schedule vacation time, she inadvertently sustained her body’s false alarms. Her delay in sleep and avoidance of positive events reinforced her belief that she was emotionally hollowed out, while each physiological surge reactivated the full sensory reliving of the ICU. The relentless flashbacks and hypervigilance convinced her that her physical vulnerability was permanent, closing the loop. The cycle finally crystallized during a shift at her restaurant. While plating a simple risotto, the clatter of a dropped pan sent her straight back to the ICU monitor’s alarm. Her chest seized, her breath shortened, and she had to step out into the walk-in freezer to steady herself. Over the past few months, this pattern had cost her promotions, strained her relationship, and left her kitchen no longer a place of creation but a minefield of bodily threats. She came to the clinic because the exhaustion had become unbearable, and though she feared she was beyond repair, she was desperately hoping to reclaim a life where she could finally trust her own body again.
